On the orders of subgroups of finite groups. We give a short account of why the number of elements of a subgroup divides the number of elements of the whole group, using a partition into cosets.

Elements of prime order. We show that when a prime divides the order of a finite group, some element of the group has exactly that prime as its order. The proof counts tuples whose product is the identity.
A note on powers modulo a prime. For a prime p and an integer a that p does not divide, the power a^(p-1) leaves remainder 1 on division by p. We also discuss Carmichael numbers.
Factorials and primality. We revisit the criterion that n is prime if and only if (n-1)! is congruent to -1 modulo n, and discuss why it is not a practical test.
Parity of odd vertices. In any finite graph the count of vertices with odd degree is even. We give a proof by summing degrees and some variants for multigraphs.
Degrees and edges. Each edge adds two to the total degree of a graph, so the degree sum is twice the number of edges.
Intermediate values of continuous maps. A real function that is continuous on a closed interval reaches every value between f(a) and f(b). We give a proof by bisection.
Secant slopes and derivatives. For a function continuous on [a,b] and differentiable inside, some interior point has derivative equal to the slope between the end points.
Bounded sequences have convergent subsequences. We review the classical argument with nested intervals and its use in compactness proofs.
Kernels and images of linear maps. For a linear map on a finite-dimensional space, the dimension of the space is the sum of the dimensions of the kernel and the image.
Unique factorisation in the integers. Every integer larger than one is a product of primes, and the product is unique apart from the order of the factors.
Infinitely many primes. Given finitely many primes, the product plus one has a prime factor that is not in the list. We collect several other proofs.
Numerical evidence on sums of two primes. We check that each even integer in a large range is a sum of two primes and estimate the number of representations.
Prime pairs with gap two. We survey the heuristics for the number of primes p below x such that p+2 is also prime.
Groups of prime order. A group whose order is a prime has no proper nontrivial subgroups, so any element other than the identity generates it.
Subgroups of index two. A subgroup that has exactly two cosets is normal, because the left and the right cosets agree.
